title: Chapter 3 — Why The Americans Display More Readiness And More Taste For General Ideas Than Their Forefathers, The English.
paragraphs: General Ideas Than Their Forefathers, The English.

The Deity does not regard the human race collectively. He surveys at a single glance, and separately, all the beings of whom mankind is composed, and he sees in each man both the resemblances that make him like his fellows and the differences that mark him off from them. God, therefore, has no need of general ideas; that is, he never feels the necessity of grouping a great many similar objects under the same form for greater convenience of thought. That is not the case with man. If the human mind were to try to examine and judge every individual case before it, the immense amount of detail would soon lead it astray and bewilder its discernment. In this tight spot, man falls back on an imperfect but necessary expedient that at once aids and reveals his weakness. Having superficially considered a certain number of objects and noted their resemblance, he gives them a common name, sets them apart, and moves on.

General ideas are no proof of the strength of the human intellect; rather, they are proof of its insufficiency. For there are in nature no beings exactly alike, no things precisely identical, nor any rules that apply indiscriminately and uniformly to several objects at once. The chief merit of general ideas is that they enable the human mind to pass a rapid judgment on a great many objects at once. But on the other hand, the notions they convey are always incomplete, and they always cause the mind to lose as much in accuracy as it gains in scope. As social bodies advance in civilization, they acquire knowledge of new facts, and they daily seize, almost without realizing it, on certain particular truths. The more truths of this kind a man grasps, the more general ideas he is naturally led to form. A multitude of particular facts cannot be seen separately without ending by revealing the common tie that binds them. Several individuals lead to the perception of the species, several species to that of the genus. The habit and the taste for general ideas will therefore always be greatest among a people of ancient cultivation and wide-ranging knowledge.
But there are other reasons that push men to generalize their ideas, or that hold them back from doing so.

The Americans are much more addicted to the use of general ideas than the English, and have a much greater taste for them. This appears very strange at first sight, when it is remembered that the two nations have the same origin, that they lived for centuries under the same laws, and that they still constantly exchange their opinions and their manners. The contrast becomes still more striking if we turn our eyes to our own part of the world and compare the two most enlightened nations in it. It would seem that the English mind can only tear itself away from the observation of particular facts reluctantly and painfully in order to rise from them to their causes, and that it generalizes only in spite of itself. Among the French, by contrast, the taste for general ideas seems to have grown into such an eager passion that it must be satisfied on every occasion. I am informed every morning when I wake that some general and eternal law has just been discovered that I had never heard of before. There is no mediocre scribbler who does not try his hand at discovering truths applicable to a great kingdom, and who is very displeased with himself if he fails to compress the human race into the space of an article. So great a dissimilarity between two very enlightened nations astonishes me. If I turn my attention back to England and observe the events there in the last half-century, I think I may affirm that a taste for general ideas is increasing in that country in proportion as its ancient constitution is weakened.

The state of civilization is therefore not enough by itself to explain what prompts the human mind to love general ideas, or what turns it away from them. When the conditions of men are very unequal, and inequality itself is the permanent state of society, individual men gradually become so unlike each other that each class takes on the appearance of a distinct race. Only one of these classes is in view at any one moment, and, losing sight of the general tie that binds them all within the vast bosom of mankind, one's observation invariably settles not on man, but on certain men. Those who live in this aristocratic state of society never, therefore, conceive very general ideas about themselves; and that is enough to imbue them with a habitual distrust of such ideas and an instinctive aversion to them. The man who lives in a democratic country, by contrast, sees around him, on every side, men differing very little from each other. He cannot turn his mind toward any one portion of mankind without his thought expanding and dilating until it embraces the whole. All the truths that apply to himself appear to him equally and in the same way applicable to each of his fellow citizens and fellow men. Having acquired the habit of generalizing his ideas in the study that absorbs him most and interests him more than others, he carries that same habit into all his pursuits. So the craving to discover general laws in everything, to bring a great many objects under a single formula, and to explain a mass of facts by a single cause, becomes an eager, and sometimes an undiscerning, passion of the human mind.

Nothing shows the truth of this proposition more clearly than the opinions of the ancients concerning their slaves. The deepest and most capacious minds of Rome and Greece were never able to reach the idea — at once so general and so simple — of the common likeness of men and of the common birthright of each to freedom. They labored to prove that slavery was in the order of nature, and that it would always exist. More than that, everything shows that those of the ancients who had passed from slavery to freedom, many of whom have left us excellent writings, themselves regarded servitude in no other light.

All the great writers of antiquity belonged to the aristocracy of masters, or at least saw that aristocracy established and uncontested before their eyes. Their minds, after spreading in several directions, were barred from further progress in this one. The advent of Jesus Christ on earth was required to teach that all members of the human race are by nature equal and alike.

In ages of equality all men are independent of each other, isolated and weak. The movements of the multitude are not permanently guided by the will of any individuals. At such times humanity seems always to advance of itself. In order to explain what is happening in the world, a man is therefore driven to look for some great causes that, acting in the same way on all his fellow creatures, impel them all involuntarily to follow the same path. This in turn naturally leads the human mind to form general ideas, and produces a taste for them.

I have already shown how the equality of conditions leads every man to investigate truths for himself. It can easily be seen that a method of this kind must imperceptibly produce a tendency toward general ideas in the human mind. When I reject the traditions of rank, profession, and birth, when I escape from the authority of example to seek out, by the single effort of my own reason, the path I should follow, I am inclined to derive the grounds of my opinions from human nature itself. This necessarily, and almost unconsciously, leads me to adopt a great many very general notions.

All I have said here explains why the English show much less readiness and taste for generalizing ideas than their American offspring, and still less than their French neighbors; and likewise why the English of today display more of these qualities than their forefathers did. The English have long been a very enlightened and very aristocratic nation. Their enlightened condition constantly urged them to generalize, while their aristocratic habits confined them to particularizing. From this arose that philosophy — at once bold and timid, broad and narrow — which has so far prevailed in England, and which still clogs and stagnates so many minds in that country.

Apart from the causes I have pointed out above, others may be discerned, less apparent but no less effective, which produce among almost every democratic people a taste, and often a passion, for general ideas. A careful distinction must be drawn between ideas of this kind. Some are the result of slow, minute, and conscientious labor of the mind, and these extend the sphere of human knowledge. Others spring up suddenly from the first rapid exercise of the wits, and produce only very superficial and very uncertain notions. Men who live in ages of equality have a great deal of curiosity and very little leisure. Their life is so practical, so confused, so excited, so active, that little time is left for thought. Such men are drawn to general ideas because these spare them the trouble of studying particulars. They contain, so to speak, a great deal in a little compass, and give a great return in a little time. If, then, on a brief and inattentive examination, a common relation is thought to be detected between certain objects, the inquiry is pushed no further. Without examining in detail how far these different objects differ or agree, they are hastily arranged under one formula, so as to move on to another subject.

One of the distinguishing features of a democratic period is the taste all men have at such times for easy success and present enjoyment. This holds in the pursuits of the intellect as in all others. Most of those who live in a time of equality are full of an ambition at once aspiring and lax: they would like to succeed brilliantly and at once, but would rather be spared great efforts in obtaining success. These conflicting tendencies lead straight to the pursuit of general ideas, by which they flatter themselves that they can cut a great figure at small expense and draw the attention of the public with very little trouble. And I do not know whether they are wrong to think so. For their readers are just as averse to investigating anything thoroughly as the writers themselves are; and what is generally sought in the productions of the mind is easy pleasure and information without labor.

If aristocratic nations do not make enough use of general ideas and often treat them with thoughtless disdain, it is true, on the other hand, that a democratic people is always ready to carry ideas of this kind to excess and to embrace them with injudicious enthusiasm.
